docs.title: cvprism init
docs.text:
First-run setup: device name, hub or spoke, vault location, watch paths.

Usage:

$ cvprism init [OPTIONS]

Options:

  • --name <str>: Device name, e.g. office-01.
  • --role <str>: hub or spoke.
  • --vault <path>: Vault folder (hub) or synced vault folder (spoke).
  • -a, --adapter <list[str]>: Sync transport (repeatable): git:<url>, gdrive:<folder>, usb, syncthing:<folder>, local:<folder>.
  • --watch <list[str]>: Project folder to watch (repeatable).
  • --no-claude-capture: Disable Claude Code session capture.
  • -y, --yes: Non-interactive; requires --name, --role, --vault.
  • --force / --no-force: Redo setup on an already configured device. [default: no-force]
  • --web: Use a setup page in your browser instead of the terminal.
  • --help: Show this message and exit.

docs.title: cvprism log
docs.text:
Record an achievement manually.

Usage:

$ cvprism log [OPTIONS] {text}

Arguments:

  • text <str>: One line describing what you did. [required]

Options:

  • -s, --skill <list[str]>: Skill name (repeatable).
  • -d, --depth <int range>: 1 used, 2 applied, 3 built, 4 led/production, 5 authored/taught. [1<=x<=5]
  • -r, --result <str>: metric:value:unit[:up|down|abs]
  • --work: Non-code achievement (paper, talk, field work, award).
  • --project <str>: Project alias (mapped to a display name in profile.yaml).
  • --raw: Skip Claude; store your words as-is.
  • --link <list[str]>: Public proof URL, e.g. a DOI, PyPI page or video (repeatable).
  • --help: Show this message and exit.

docs.title: cvprism status
docs.text:
Show this device's capture and sync state.

Usage:

$ cvprism status [OPTIONS]

Options:

  • --help: Show this message and exit.

docs.title: cvprism install
docs.text:
Register capture hooks, skills and the background agent (all reversible with cvprism uninstall).

Usage:

$ cvprism install [OPTIONS]

Options:

  • --no-claude: Skip the Claude Code SessionEnd hook.
  • --no-git: Skip the global git hook dispatcher.
  • --no-skills: Skip installing /cv-log and /cv-build skills.
  • --no-service: Skip the background agent at login.
  • --dry-run: Show what would change, change nothing.
  • --help: Show this message and exit.

docs.title: cvprism uninstall
docs.text:
Remove hooks, skills and the login agent, restoring previous settings. Data is kept.

Usage:

$ cvprism uninstall [OPTIONS]

Options:

  • --no-service: Leave the login agent registration alone.
  • --help: Show this message and exit.

docs.text:
Process queued capture jobs once (the agent does this automatically).

Usage:

$ cvprism worker [OPTIONS]

Options:

  • --help: Show this message and exit.

docs.title: cvprism agent
docs.text:
Background capture agent: folder watcher + queue worker. Started at login by cvprism install.

Usage:

$ cvprism agent [OPTIONS]

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
No terminal?

Double-click start.bat (Windows) or run ./start.sh with no arguments. Setup and the cvprism app open in your browser.

You need Python 3.10+ (3.12+ for PDF output) and, for automatic capture, Claude Code. There is no database and no server.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/sayantanonfire/cvprism.git
cd cvprism
./start.sh          # Windows: start.bat

The start script creates a private Python environment in your user data folder, installs cvprism, and starts setup. It works the same from a USB stick: once installed, nothing depends on the stick.

Setup asks four things: a device name, whether this computer is the hub (where CVs are built) or a spoke, where your private vault lives, and which project folders to watch. Prefer a browser page? Run cvprism init --web.

Your vault is private

The vault holds your career evidence. Keep it outside the cvprism code folder. cvprism refuses to create it there.

docs.title: Bring in what you already have
docs.text:
cvprism import-linkedin ~/Downloads/Basic_LinkedInDataExport.zip   # positions, education, certifications, skills
cvprism import-cv ~/Documents/old_cv.docx                          # bullets become cards
cvprism import-orcid 0000-0002-1825-0097                           # publications into pubs.bib

Imported cards are flagged for review, because they are self-reported. Skills that were only listed on LinkedIn become depth-1 cards: cvprism knows about them, but they don't appear on a CV until you have stronger evidence.

docs.title: Turn on automatic capture
docs.text:
cvprism install --dry-run    # shows every change first
cvprism install              # Claude Code hook, git hook, /cv-log skill, background agent

Everything is reversible with cvprism uninstall, which restores your previous git and Claude Code settings exactly.

From now on:

  • When a Claude Code session ends, a summary of the skills and methods used becomes candidate cards a few minutes later.
  • Git commits and new dependencies in watched folders are batched into the same process.
  • /cv-log inside Claude Code, or cvprism log "..." in a terminal, records anything else: papers, talks, field work.

docs.title: Build a CV
docs.text:
cvprism build --role applied-ai
cvprism build --jd https://example.com/jobs/123

See Building CVs.

docs.title: Many computers, one hub
docs.text: Pick one computer as the hub. It keeps the vault and builds CVs. Every other computer is a spoke: it records your work and sends cards to the hub. Spokes never talk to each other.

docs.title: Choose how cards travel
docs.text:
Transport Use it when Set it up with Private git repo Computers on different networks --adapter git:git@github.com:you/cvprism-vault.git Synced folder You already use Google Drive, OneDrive or Dropbox --adapter gdrive:~/Google Drive/cvprism USB stick Offline or locked-down machines --adapter usb (create a cvprism-dropbox folder on the stick) Syncthing Computers on the same network, no cloud --adapter syncthing:~/Sync/cvprism

You can use several at once. A card that arrives twice by different routes is stored once.

docs.title: Set up
docs.text:
# on the hub
cvprism init --name home-pc --role hub --vault ~/cvprism-vault --adapter git:git@github.com:you/cvprism-vault.git --yes
cvprism sync

# on each spoke
cvprism init --name office-01 --role spoke --adapter git:git@github.com:you/cvprism-vault.git --yes
cvprism sync

The background agent (cvprism install) syncs every 15 minutes and immediately when a USB drop-box appears. Offline? Cards wait in the local outbox and go out when any transport is reachable. cvprism status shows the backlog.

docs.title: Common tasks
docs.text:
• Replace the hub: run cvprism hub promote --vault ~/cvprism-vault on the new computer. It rebuilds everything from the transports. The old hub steps down by itself the next time it syncs.
  • Hide a card from CVs: cvprism suppress <card-id> on the hub. History is kept.
  • Erase a card everywhere: cvprism purge <card-id>. Git history keeps old commits; cvprism prints the git filter-repo command if you need those gone too.

How this stays conflict-free: Sync protocol.

docs.title: Verifiable CVs
docs.text: AI made every CV look polished, so recruiters stopped trusting polish. cvprism makes honesty checkable instead: lines with public proof carry a blue link to the work itself, every line is graded by how strong its proof is, and private work keeps its skills without exposing anything.

docs.title: What the reader sees
docs.text:
• In the body: bullets with public proof end with a short blue link, for example github.com/you/flood-copilot/commit/9fceb02 or doi.org/10.1016/…. The visible text is the real URL (no icons), so it survives ATS parsing.
  • Private work: ends with (private repository). The skill and the achievement are fully listed; only the code is not public.
  • Local work: no label at all.
  • Last page, "Evidence": every line with its proof level, link (or "private repository" / "local work" / "no link yet") and the date it was captured.
Proof level Meaning Public proof Anyone can click and see the work Third-party confirmed Published with a DOI Captured Recorded automatically at the time (Claude Code session, commit, project folder) Self-reported You entered it (manual log or import)

docs.title: Mark your projects once
docs.text:
cvprism project set flood-copilot --public --url https://github.com/you/flood-copilot
cvprism project set client-dam --private --display "Dam-break study for a utility"
cvprism project set thesis-code --local
cvprism project list

Visibility lives on the project, so making a repo public later adds links to every past line from it at the next build. Nothing needs re-capturing.

On each computer, tell cvprism which folder belongs to which project, so captured commits and sessions are tagged automatically:

cvprism project map flood-copilot D:\work\flood-copilot

Only the project alias travels between computers. Repository URLs exist only on your hub, and only for projects you mark public.

docs.title: Add proof that isn't in git
docs.text:
cvprism log "Presented flood copilot at EGU 2026" --skill science-communication --depth 5 --work \
  --link https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=...
cvprism link c_9a59b3fedb34160f https://pypi.org/project/hydrotools/

Links must be public https:// addresses. Publications from BibTeX/ORCID link through their DOI automatically.

docs.title: Build with proof
docs.text:
cvprism build --role applied-ai --check-links

--check-links opens every link first and drops any that don't load, so you never send a dead link.

docs.title: Publish a verify page (optional)
docs.text:
Add a target to profile.yaml: a public GitHub Pages repository you own.

verify:
  repo: git@github.com:you/you.github.io.git
  path: cv
  url: https://you.github.io/cv

Then build with --publish. cvprism writes a small page (evidence table, QR code, file fingerprint) and pushes it to that repository. Your CV gets a "Verify this CV" link in the header, and the Word file includes the QR code.

Anyone can confirm a CV file is exactly the one you built:

cvprism verify cv.pdf --manifest https://you.github.io/cv/manifest.json

What the fingerprint proves

The fingerprint proves the file was not changed after cvprism built it. It does not prove the claims: the public links do that. The verify page says this in plain words.

docs.title: Sign your CV (optional)
docs.text:
Prove a CV came from you, using the SSH key you already use for GitHub:

verify:
  repo: git@github.com:you/you.github.io.git
  url: https://you.github.io/cv
  signing_key: ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

cvprism build --role academic --sign --publish

Anyone can then check both the file and its author:

cvprism verify cv.pdf --manifest https://you.github.io/cv/manifest.json --github you

The signature only needs OpenSSH, so it can be checked without cvprism (see the open specification).

docs.title: Why this design
docs.text: See ADR-015, ADR-017 and the design spec.

docs.title: Evidence-linked CV, version 1 (open specification)
docs.text:
• Status: Draft standard, implemented by cvprism 1.2
  • Licence: Apache-2.0. Anyone may implement it, in any tool.
  • Schema: manifest.schema.json (JSON Schema 2020-12)

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Hiring has a trust problem: AI made every CV look polished, so polish stopped meaning anything. An evidence-linked CV ships with a machine-readable manifest that says, for every line, what proof backs it. The CV files carry fingerprints, and the manifest can optionally be signed with the author's existing SSH key. A recruiter, an ATS or a verification service can check all of this without trusting the tool that made the CV.

The format is deliberately small, so that any CV builder can produce it and any ATS can read it.

docs.title: 1. The manifest
docs.text:
manifest.json, UTF-8, published next to the CV (for example on the author's own website):

Field Required Meaning v ✓ 1 name ✓ Person's name as on the CV headline Headline/role title on the CV role Identifier of the CV variant built ✓ RFC 3339 time the CV was produced file ✓ Main CV file name the sha256 refers to sha256 ✓ SHA-256 (hex) of file files ✓ Map of every produced CV file name → SHA-256 bullets ✓ One entry per CV line, below

Each bullets[] entry:

Field Required Meaning text ✓ The line as printed (without its link) level ✓ Proof level (section 2) links Public https:// URLs proving the line label Human label when no link exists, e.g. private repository date YYYY-MM-DD when the underlying evidence was first recorded cites Opaque IDs of the author's evidence records section Where the line appears (pos, proj, work)

docs.title: 2. Proof levels
docs.text:
A producer MUST compute levels from evidence. It MUST NOT let the author choose them.

Level Rule public At least one link a third party can open that shows the work itself confirmed Confirmed by an independent party (e.g. a DOI-registered publication, an issued credential) captured Recorded automatically by a tool at the time the work happened self-reported Entered by the author

Private work is first-class. Lines from closed-source or confidential work MUST be allowed, without links, typically labelled private repository. A consumer MUST NOT treat the absence of a link as evidence of falsehood.

docs.title: 3. Links on the printed CV
docs.text:
• Links SHOULD appear as visible URL text, not icons, so ATS parsers keep them.
  • A link MUST point at the work (a commit, release, paper, video), not at a profile page that merely restates the claim.
  • Producers SHOULD check that links open before publishing.

docs.title: 4. Fingerprints
docs.text: sha256 and files let anyone confirm a received file is byte-for-byte the one described. A fingerprint proves integrity, not truth, and consumers SHOULD present it that way.

docs.title: 5. Signatures (optional)
docs.text:
• manifest.json.sig is an OpenSSH signature (ssh-keygen -Y sign) over the exact bytes of manifest.json, with namespace cvprism-cv.
  • Verification uses the author's public SSH keys, for example those GitHub publishes at https://github.com/<user>.keys:
echo "<user> namespaces=\"cvprism-cv\" <public key>" > allowed_signers
ssh-keygen -Y verify -f allowed_signers -I <user> -n cvprism-cv -s manifest.json.sig < manifest.json
  • A valid signature proves the manifest was produced by whoever controls that key. It still does not prove the claims; the links do.

docs.title: 6. Verifying a CV, step by step
docs.text:
1. Fetch manifest.json (and .sig if present) from the URL printed on the CV.
  2. Compare the received file's SHA-256 with files.
  3. Optionally verify the signature against the author's published keys.
  4. Open the links for the lines that matter to the role.

With cvprism: cvprism verify cv.pdf --manifest https://you.github.io/cv/manifest.json --github you.

docs.title: 7. Versioning
docs.text: Additive fields keep v: 1. Any change in meaning increments v, and consumers MUST reject versions they do not understand.

docs.title: Verifiable CV: evidence links and proof levels
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-11-28
  • Status: Approved by owner, in implementation
  • Decision record: ADR-015

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Recruiters no longer trust CVs: AI polish made every CV look equally good, so polish stopped being a signal. cvprism already refuses unsupported claims, but a recruiter cannot see that. A cvprism CV must make its honesty visible and checkable, without exposing private or client work and without ever dropping skills learned in closed-source projects.

docs.title: Decisions (from brainstorming)
docs.text:
1. Link sources: automatic, opt-in per project; manual links for anything else.
  2. Verification: an Evidence appendix in every CV, plus an optional static verify page on a GitHub Pages repo the user owns.
  3. In the body: a short blue link at the end of bullets with public proof. No symbols.
  4. Private work is first-class: skills from private or local projects always appear. Only the link differs.

docs.title: Visibility rules
docs.text:
Project visibility Body shows Evidence page shows public (+ url) Bullet + blue link (commit, PR or project URL) Link private Bullet + (private repository) "private repository" local or unset Bullet only "local work"

Spokes never send repository URLs. Only the hub's profile.yaml knows a project's URL, and only when marked public. Because visibility lives on the project and links are resolved at build time, making a repo public later adds links to every past card without re-capture.

docs.title: Proof levels (computed, never typed)
docs.text: Level Rule public At least one resolvable public link (public project, card lnk, or a link in vault/links.jsonl) confirmed Publication with a DOI (BibTeX/ORCID) captured src is claude_session, git_commit or watcher self-reported src is manual or import

docs.title: Components
docs.text: Unit Responsibility compile/evidence.py Repo URL normalisation, commit URLs per host (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket), proof resolution per card and per bullet, link checking (injectable fetcher) compile/verify.py Manifest (PDF SHA-256, per-bullet proof), static verify page, QR code, publish to a git repo, verify comparison capture/projects.py Device path → project mapping; tagging captured cards with ctx CLI project set/map/list, link, log --link, build --check-links --publish, verify Renderers Blue links in PDF (RenderCV colors.links), DOCX (hyperlink runs) and Markdown; (private repository) label; Evidence section; "Verify" header link

docs.title: Data changes
docs.text:
• Card: optional lnk (list of https URLs, max 5, not part of the ID hash).
  • Profile projects[]: visibility, url. Profile verify: {repo, path, url}.
  • Device: projects: [{ctx, path}].
  • Hub: vault/links.jsonl (append-only {id, url, t}).
  • Build: build.json gains pdf_sha256; manifest.json lists every bullet with cites, level and link.

docs.title: Honesty and limits
docs.text:
• Links are never invented: they come from a public project's real commit reference, a URL the user supplied, or a DOI.
  • The fingerprint proves the PDF was not altered after the build. It does not prove claims true, and the verify page says so.
  • The QR code ships on the verify page and in DOCX first. In-PDF QR needs a custom RenderCV theme (follow-up).
  • The Evidence page is an appendix: the page limit for the CV body is limits.pages, and the build allows one extra page for the appendix.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: Unit tests for every unit above, an end-to-end build with mixed public/private/local projects, publish + verify against a local bare repo, and a visual check of the demo PDF.
